explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Lot, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 14:12), invites the two visitors to wash their feet and spend the night. They answer, “we will spend the night in the square.” (Genesis 19:2) So their first answer is no, and it takes Lot insisting so strongly before they follow him into his house (Genesis 19:3).

That's it, friend. Lot, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 14:12), invites them in, and they answer, “we will spend the night in the square.” (Genesis 19:2) They don't say yes right away. Lot has to insist so strongly that they finally follow him into his house (Genesis 19:3).

Yes, a feast! Verse 3 says Lot “…prepared a feast for them and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.” (Genesis 19:3) That's some serious hosting for guests who first said no thanks. I respect a host who goes all out, and I'd bring the cookies.

A gift is a kind thought, friend, but that's not what the text says. It says Lot “…prepared a feast for them and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.” (Genesis 19:3) Guests who first said they'd spend the night in the square end up at his table. I'd say Lot's insisting paid off.

A lamp would be handy in the evening, friend, but the text never mentions one. What Lot does is prepare a feast for them. He also bakes unleavened bread, and the guests eat (Genesis 19:3). That's a table, not a light fixture.

explanations.answer: Steps outside and shuts the door
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. “Lot went outside to meet them, shutting the door behind him.” (Genesis 19:6) He goes out to face the whole crowd, and his guests stay behind that door. Honestly, I'd have needed a minute and a cookie first. That's a lot of nerve.

explanations.answer: Bars the door from the inside
explanations.explanation: That would keep him inside, but it isn't what the text says. Lot does the opposite: he “…went outside to meet them, shutting the door behind him.” (Genesis 19:6) So he's on the outside with the crowd, not safe behind a bar. Quite a move.

explanations.answer: Calls down to them from the roof
explanations.explanation: The text never puts Lot on a roof, friend. It says he “…went outside to meet them, shutting the door behind him.” (Genesis 19:6) He goes out to them and shuts the door. That makes his next words even bolder.

True! “Please, my brothers…” he pleaded, “don’t do such a wicked thing!” (Genesis 19:7) Lot calls what they want wicked, right to their faces. That takes real nerve with a whole city outside his door.
Actually, that one is true. The text says, “Please, my brothers…” he pleaded, “don’t do such a wicked thing!” (Genesis 19:7) Lot does speak up, and he calls it wicked. So he does plead with them.

explanations.answer: He came as a foreigner and now acts like a judge
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. They say, “This one came here as a foreigner, and he is already acting like a judge!” (Genesis 19:9) They're saying he's an outsider telling them what to do. Then they threaten to treat him worse than his guests.

explanations.answer: He is a spy who came in with the strangers
explanations.explanation: Spy is a good guess, but the crowd never says it. What they say is, “This one came here as a foreigner, and he is already acting like a judge!” (Genesis 19:9) Their complaint is that he's an outsider acting like a judge.

explanations.answer: He owes the whole city a debt he never paid
explanations.explanation: No debt collectors in this scene, friend. The crowd says, “This one came here as a foreigner, and he is already acting like a judge!” (Genesis 19:9) Their complaint is that a foreigner is acting like a judge. Money never comes up.

explanations.answer: Pull Lot inside and shut the door
explanations.explanation: Yes! “…the men inside reached out, pulled Lot into the house with them, and shut the door.” (Genesis 19:10) The crowd had just pressed in and moved to break down the door (Genesis 19:9). Lot gets pulled to safety right then. I'd like a friend who grabs me at exactly the right second.

explanations.answer: Step outside to face the crowd
explanations.explanation: That's a brave guess, but they stay put. The text says the men inside “…reached out, pulled Lot into the house with them, and shut the door.” (Genesis 19:10) Lot is the one who gets brought in. The two guests stay at the door and don't go out.

explanations.answer: Slip out through the back way
explanations.explanation: A back way would be a smart plan, but the text never mentions one. It says the men inside “…reached out, pulled Lot into the house with them, and shut the door.” (Genesis 19:10) That's what happens: Lot is pulled in and the door is shut.

That's right, friend. The men inside “…struck the men at the entrance, young and old, with blindness, so that they wearied themselves trying to find the door.” (Genesis 19:11) A moment before, the crowd was pressing in to break that door down (Genesis 19:9). Now they're wearing themselves out just trying to find it.

Sickness is a fair guess, friend, but that's not what the text says. The men at the entrance were struck “…with blindness, so that they wearied themselves trying to find the door.” (Genesis 19:11) Blindness is what kept them from finding that door. Silence would stop the shouting, friend, but it wouldn't stop them from finding the door. The text says they were struck “…with blindness, so that they wearied themselves trying to find the door.” (Genesis 19:11) It was the blindness that kept them from finding it.

explanations.answer: They are about to destroy the city
explanations.explanation: Yes. The two men say, “…we are about to destroy this place. For the outcry to the LORD against its people is so great that He has sent us to destroy it.” (Genesis 19:13) That's why Lot has to move fast and get his people out. This is the outcry the LORD told Abraham about (Genesis 18:20).

explanations.answer: The crowd will be back at dawn
explanations.explanation: The crowd is a fair worry, friend, but it's not what the men say. Their reason is, “…we are about to destroy this place.” (Genesis 19:13) They say the outcry to the LORD against its people is so great that He has sent them to destroy it. Nothing in the text mentions the crowd coming back at dawn.

explanations.answer: A famine is coming to the plain
explanations.explanation: No famine in this passage, friend. The men say, “…we are about to destroy this place. For the outcry to the LORD against its people is so great that He has sent us to destroy it.” (Genesis 19:13) The reason is the destruction, and they tell Lot to get his family out before it comes.

That's right, friend. “…his sons-in-law thought he was joking.” (Genesis 19:14) Lot has just told them the LORD is about to destroy the city, and they don't take it seriously. I think this one is heavy, because the warning was real. And the story isn't over.

explanations.answer: They run to warn the city
explanations.explanation: Nobody runs anywhere in this verse, friend. The text says, “…his sons-in-law thought he was joking.” (Genesis 19:14) They don't take the warning seriously. It's a short verse, but a heavy one.

explanations.answer: They leave with him that night
explanations.explanation: I wish that were how it went. But “…his sons-in-law thought he was joking.” (Genesis 19:14) They don't leave with Lot. When daybreak comes, the angels tell Lot to take his wife and his two daughters who are there (Genesis 19:15).

Yes, “…when Lot hesitated, the men grabbed his hand and the hands of his wife and his two daughters.” (Genesis 19:16) So he slows down instead of hurrying. I can't judge, because I've hit snooze on way smaller emergencies than this one.

Hiding would be a move, but the text doesn't say it. It says, “…when Lot hesitated, the men grabbed his hand and the hands of his wife and his two daughters.” (Genesis 19:16) So Lot hesitates, and the men take hold of the family. They don't go looking for anyone hiding.

Praying is a good thing to do, friend, but the text doesn't put it here. It says, “…when Lot hesitated, the men grabbed his hand and the hands of his wife and his two daughters.” (Genesis 19:16) The word for Lot at that moment is hesitated. That's when the men take hold of their hands.

Yes, compassion. The men “…led them safely out of the city, because of the LORD’s compassion for them.” (Genesis 19:16) Lot is slow, and they're still led out by the hand. That tells me a lot about the LORD.
That's a close guess, but the text uses a different word. They led them out “…because of the LORD’s compassion for them.” (Genesis 19:16) The family was led out by the hand because of His compassion.

The text doesn't say command here, friend. It says they led them “…safely out of the city, because of the LORD’s compassion for them.” (Genesis 19:16) It's compassion that gets them out, and the men take them by the hand to do it.

That's right. The man says, “Run for your lives! Do not look back, and do not stop anywhere on the plain!” (Genesis 19:17) Keep your eyes forward and keep moving. Hold on to that one, because it matters in a few verses.

Nobody tells them to stay quiet. The man says, “Run for your lives! Do not look back, and do not stop anywhere on the plain!” (Genesis 19:17) The other order is not to look back. Talking is not mentioned.
Packing is not mentioned, friend. What the man says is, “Run for your lives! Do not look back, and do not stop anywhere on the plain!” (Genesis 19:17) So the other order is not to look back.

explanations.answer: To flee to a small town nearby
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Lot says, “…there is a town nearby where I can flee, and it is a small place.” (Genesis 19:20) He asks to flee to that town instead of the mountains. Then he asks, “…is it not a small place?” and adds, “Then my life will be saved.”

explanations.answer: To go back for his sons-in-law
explanations.explanation: Going back isn't what he asks for. Lot says, “…there is a town nearby where I can flee, and it is a small place.” (Genesis 19:20) He asks to flee to that town. The sons-in-law already thought he was joking (Genesis 19:14).

explanations.answer: To hide out in Abraham's tents
explanations.explanation: Abraham's tents don't come up in Lot's request, friend. What he asks for is a town: “…there is a town nearby where I can flee, and it is a small place.” (Genesis 19:20) He wants a nearby town that's small.

Not this time. The man answers, “Very well, I will grant this request as well, and will not demolish the town you indicate.” (Genesis 19:21) Lot asks, and he gets a yes. The LORD's compassion for him is still going.

Right! The man says, “Very well,” he answered, “I will grant this request as well, and will not demolish the town you indicate.” (Genesis 19:21) Lot gets a yes. Then comes the order to hurry, because the man can't do anything until Lot gets there (Genesis 19:22).

Yes, that's what the text says. “…Lot’s wife looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.” (Genesis 19:26) The order had been, “Do not look back…” (Genesis 19:17) This is a heavy verse, so let's take it in quietly.

explanations.answer: Smoke rising like smoke from a furnace
explanations.explanation: That's right. Abraham “…saw the smoke rising from the land like smoke from a furnace.” (Genesis 19:28) He's standing in the very place where he had stood before the LORD. It's a quiet, heavy picture.

explanations.answer: A flood covering the whole plain
explanations.explanation: A flood is a common guess, but that's not what Abraham sees. The text says, “…he saw the smoke rising from the land like smoke from a furnace.” (Genesis 19:28) What he sees is smoke over the plain. Fire and sulfur came down from the LORD (Genesis 19:24).

explanations.answer: Dust rising from a marching army
explanations.explanation: No army in this scene, friend. Abraham “…saw the smoke rising from the land like smoke from a furnace.” (Genesis 19:28) It's smoke from the land of the plain.

Yes, friend. “…He remembered Abraham, and He brought Lot out of the catastrophe that destroyed the cities where he had lived.” (Genesis 19:29) Lot is Abraham's nephew (Genesis 14:12). Earlier, Abraham had spoken up to the LORD about Sodom (Genesis 18:23-32). The verse puts God remembering Abraham right beside Lot being brought out.

Sarah is Abraham's wife (Genesis 17:19), but this verse doesn't name her. It says, “…He remembered Abraham, and He brought Lot out of the catastrophe that destroyed the cities where he had lived.” (Genesis 19:29) So the name in the blank is Abraham. Lot is Abraham's nephew (Genesis 14:12).

Noah is from an earlier story, so that's a fair guess, friend. But this verse names someone else: “…He remembered Abraham, and He brought Lot out of the catastrophe that destroyed the cities where he had lived.” (Genesis 19:29) Lot is Abraham's nephew (Genesis 14:12). So the blank is Abraham.

explanations.answer: He is afraid to stay there

The text doesn't say that, friend. It says Lot “…settled in the mountains—for he was afraid to stay in Zoar…” (Genesis 19:30) The reason it gives is that Lot was afraid to stay. It doesn't say anything about the town turning him away.
